extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens and voters considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution (general public interested in constitutional design).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentative criteria for judging whether particular powers granted by the proposed U.S. Constitution are necessary, proper, and safely limited; addresses classes of federal powers and interpretive principles. Aimed at informing voters' ratification decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a power for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: When conferring power, the first question is whether such a power be necessary to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide if power is a necessary means to a necessary end; accept that every political advantage carries some unavoidable inconvenience and potential for abuse; choose the greater, not the perfect, good; if necessary, provide effective guards against perversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against perversion of conferred powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a power is necessary and therefore conferred, the next concern is to guard as effectually as possible against its being perverted to public detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional limits, terms, and structures (e.g., appropriations term limits) to diminish the likelihood and effects of abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify powers by object when assessing scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Review powers by grouping them according to their objects: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony and intercourse among the States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of the States from injurious acts; (6) provisions for giving efficacy to these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using such classification clarifies whether powers are necessary and appropriately scoped for federal administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to declare war
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to declare war is necessary and properly placed in the general government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extensive proof needed because existing Confederation already vested it; treat it as a primitive object of civil society tied to national defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to raise armies and equip fleets
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to provide armies and fleets is necessarily involved in the power to declare war and the power of self-defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such powers follow from the need to execute the war-making/self-defense function effectively; cannot be meaningfully severed from the power to defend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite power to raise troops and maintain forces in peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to give an indefinite power to raise troops and maintain them in peace as well as war must be judged by necessity — one cannot safely limit defensive force if one cannot limit the force of offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting defensive preparations while other nations can prepare offense is impractical; constitutional restraint should avoid creating precedents that force repeated usurpations; balance readiness and liberty prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as a safeguard against dangerous standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A united America reduces the pretext and need for dangerous standing peace establishments; disunion would lead to more and larger standing armies in the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue from historical examples (e.g., Europe, Rome) that disunion invites militarization; preserve union to minimize necessity of extensive peace establishments and related dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit appropriations term for military support as a check
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the term for which revenue may be appropriated to army support (two years in the Constitution) is a clear precaution against danger from standing armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare with British practice: though Britain in practice votes annually, its Constitution places no formal limit; the American Constitution imposes a two-year statutory limit which constrains legislative discretion more than no limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional prohibitions that preclude preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impractical to prohibit readiness for war in peacetime (e.g., prohibiting preparations) unless all nations' preparations could be prohibited likewise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional rules should not fetter necessary defensive preparations; such prohibitions would be futile and produce harmful usurpations later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to provide and maintain a navy
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to provide and maintain a navy is necessary and particularly salutary, being a principal source of security against foreign danger with less risk to domestic liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Union will be the source of maritime strength, naval batteries are unlikely to be turned against domestic liberties; maritime defense especially benefits coastal states (e.g., New York).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate and call forth the militia
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to regulate and call forth the militia is necessary and has been previously vindicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider militia regulation part of national defense apparatus complementing standing forces and navy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to levy and borrow money (taxation and finance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to levy and borrow money is the sinew of national defense and is necessary in both the extent and form provided by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxation must be able to adapt to changes in commerce and population; reliance solely on external taxes (imports) is insufficient and variable as domestic industry and population evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret general welfare phrase in light of enumerated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The power 'to lay and collect taxes... to pay the debts, and provide for the common defense and general welfare' does not amount to an unlimited commission to legislate in all cases; particular enumerations following the general phrase qualify its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give meaning to both general phrases and specific enumerations: treat the recital of particulars as explanatory and limiting rather than redundant; avoid construing the general clause to swallow separately enumerated powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to make treaties and appoint ambassadors/consuls
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors and other public ministers (including consuls) is proper and improves upon the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding appointment/receipt of 'other public ministers and consuls' corrects Confederation defects where 'ambassador' alone was too narrow; consuls are necessary for commercial relations and lesser diplomatic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to define and punish piracies and felonies on the high seas and offenses against the law of nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal authority to define and punish piracies, felonies on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations is necessary for uniformity and to prevent any single member from embroiling the Confederacy with foreign nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative definitions are needed for certainty and uniformity because common law/statute definitions vary among states and nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of foreign commerce by the federal government
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of foreign commerce properly belongs to the federal government and has been discussed elsewhere as essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central regulation prevents states from undermining national commercial policy and avoids inconsistent practices that would exacerbate animosities and trade retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prohibit importation of slaves after 1808 (compromise principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postponing the power to prohibit importation of slaves until 1808 is a political compromise but is still a significant point in favor of humanity, enabling eventual termination of the traffic within twenty years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the delay as a pragmatic gain rather than a criminal toleration; expect discouragement and possible abolition through majority action before the terminal date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate commerce among the States and with Indian tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: A superintending federal authority over reciprocal trade among States (and commerce with Indian tribes) is necessary to prevent burdensome inter-state imposts and resulting animosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Switzerland, Germany, Netherlands) show that lack of central regulation produces harmful tolls/customs and interstate friction; federal regulation protects commerce and harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to coin money and regulate its value, including foreign coin
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal power to coin money and regulate its value (and that of foreign coin) supplies omissions in the Confederation and ensures uniformity in currency value across States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjecting foreign coin to varying state regulations could destroy uniform value; federal standardization avoids this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to punish counterfeiting of current coin and public securities
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment of counterfeiting both the current coin and public securities belongs to the authority charged with securing the value of the national currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is naturally paired with coinage authority to preserve public credit and monetary stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to fix standards of weights and measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation of weights and measures is transferred to the federal government to secure uniformity for commerce and exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like coin regulation, uniform measures prevent confusion and fraud in interstate commercial dealings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish a uniform rule of naturalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to establish a uniform rule of naturalization is necessary to remove the confusion created by divergent state rules (e.g., 'free inhabitants' vs 'free citizens'), which can cause legal and civil difficulties across state lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform naturalization prevents situations where an alien naturalized in one state would have rights in another state that contradict local qualifications, which could produce serious legal and political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish uniform laws of bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform bankruptcy laws are intimately connected with regulation of commerce and will prevent many frauds where parties or property move between states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central bankruptcy laws reduce opportunities for forum-shopping and inconsistent treatment of debtors/creditors across state lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to prescribe proof and interstate effect of public acts/records/judicial proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal power to prescribe how public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved and the effect they shall have in other States is an improvement on the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such power can be especially convenient on borders, preventing sudden transfers of property or process from evading justice by crossing jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to establish post offices and post roads
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to establish post offices and post roads is harmless and may, if managed well, become productive of great public convenience by facilitating intercourse between States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage judicious management; view this provision as benign and useful infrastructure for national communication and unity.
